sectionTitle: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
topic: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)

specStatements.text: A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.
The pressure in fluids causes a force normal (at right angles) to any surface.
The pressure at the surface of a fluid can be calculated using the equation:
pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)
[p = F/A]
pressure, p, in pascals, Pa
force, F, in newtons, N
area, A, in metres squared, m^2
The pressure due to a column of liquid can be calculated using the equation:
pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
[p = h ρ g]
pressure, p, in pascals, Pa
height of the column, h, in metres, m
density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m^3
gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.)
Students should be able to explain why, in a liquid, pressure at a point increases with the height of the column of liquid above that point and with the density of the liquid.
Students should be able to calculate the differences in pressure at different depths in a liquid.
A partially (or totally) submerged object experiences a greater pressure on the bottom surface than on the top surface. This creates a resultant force upwards. This force is called the upthrust.
Students should be able to describe the factors which influence floating and sinking.
The atmosphere is a thin layer (relative to the size of the Earth) of air round the Earth. The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude.

Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure. The number of air molecules (and so the weight of air) above a surface decreases as the height of the surface above ground level increases. So as height increases there is always less air above a surface than there is at a lower height. So atmospheric pressure decreases with an increase in height.
Students should be able to:
• describe a simple model of the Earth’s atmosphere and of atmospheric pressure
• explain why atmospheric pressure varies with height above a surface.

scopeNotes.statement: In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every calculating item in this topic that uses p = h ρ g prints the value of g inside the stem (g = 9.8 N/kg). No item requires a student to recall g, and no key can be reached only by assuming a value. Where a student substitutes 10 N/kg in place of the stated value, that appears as a distractor (m14) and never as the correct option.

concepts.definition: A substance that can flow. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas, so gases as well as liquids exert pressure on the surfaces they touch.
The force acting normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface. Pressure is measured in pascals, Pa.
At right angles to the surface. The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface the fluid is in contact with, whatever the angle of that surface.
The unit of pressure. One pascal is one newton acting normal to each square metre of surface, so 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

concepts.term: Pressure at the surface of a fluid
concepts.definition: Calculated with pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface), that is p = F/A, with F in newtons and A in metres squared.
The area of the surface over which the normal force is spread. For a fixed force, a larger area of contact gives a smaller pressure.

concepts.term: Pressure due to a column of liquid
concepts.definition: Calculated with pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength, that is p = h ρ g.
The mass of a material per unit volume, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³. A denser liquid gives a greater pressure at the same depth.
The vertical height of liquid above the point of interest, in metres, m. It is the height of liquid above the point, not the width of the container.
The force of gravity on each kilogram of mass, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is given in any calculation in this topic.
The extra pressure between two points in a liquid, found from the difference in height of the two points: Δp = Δh ρ g.
The resultant upward force on a partially or totally submerged object, caused by the pressure on its bottom surface being greater than the pressure on its top surface.
An object floats when the upthrust can balance its weight. An object whose density is less than the density of the liquid floats; a denser object sinks.
A thin layer of air round the Earth, thin compared with the size of the Earth, which gets less dense with increasing altitude.
The pressure caused by air molecules colliding with a surface. It comes from the weight of the air above that surface.
Height above ground level. As altitude increases there is less air above a surface, so atmospheric pressure decreases.

misconceptions.question: Is air a fluid?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas, so air is a fluid and exerts pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Only liquids are fluids; a gas is not a fluid because it cannot be poured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'fluid' means a runny liquid, and the word is printed on drink and medicine bottles, never on anything gaseous.
misconceptions.correction: In physics a fluid is anything that can flow. Gases flow, so a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.

misconceptions.question: Is sand a fluid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sand is a solid made of grains; a fluid is a liquid or a gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that can be poured is a fluid, so dry sand and sugar count as fluids.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pouring is the visible test students apply, and powders pour just as liquids do.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines a fluid as a liquid or a gas. Powders are solids, however easily they pour.

misconceptions.question: In which direction does a gas press on the wall of its container?
misconceptions.correct: Normal to the wall, that is at right angles to it, pushing outwards.
misconceptions.misconception: Fluid pressure acts vertically downwards, because the fluid's weight pulls it down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is first met as an object resting on the ground, where the force really is vertically downwards.
misconceptions.correction: The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface, so on a vertical or sloping wall the force is not vertical.

misconceptions.question: A liquid presses on a sloping wall. Which way does the force act?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to the sloping wall at every point on it.
misconceptions.misconception: The force acts along the surface, in the direction the fluid is flowing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture water sliding down a wall and assume the push follows the flow.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure produces a force normal to the surface. Flow direction does not set the direction of that force.

misconceptions.question: A force is spread over a larger area. What happens to the pressure?
misconceptions.correct: The pressure decreases, because pressure = force normal to a surface / area of that surface.
misconceptions.misconception: A larger area means a larger pressure, because the force is acting over more surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More area' feels like 'more of everything', and students do not track that area is on the bottom of the fraction.
misconceptions.correction: Area divides the force. For a fixed normal force, doubling the area halves the pressure.

misconceptions.question: How do you write the equation for pressure at the surface of a fluid?
misconceptions.correct: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)
misconceptions.misconception: The equation is pressure = area divided by force normal to the surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the equation is a division but not which quantity goes on top, so they invert it.
misconceptions.correction: Force is on the top of the fraction and area on the bottom: p = F/A.

misconceptions.question: A 2.0 kg brick rests on a bench. What value of F goes into p = F/A?
misconceptions.correct: The weight of the brick in newtons, found from its mass and the gravitational field strength.
misconceptions.misconception: When finding the force F for p = F/A from a mass, students mishandle the mass-to-weight conversion: putting the mass value straight in as the force, using g itself as the force, or dividing the mass by g instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and the mass is the number printed in the question.
misconceptions.correction: F is a force in newtons. Convert mass to weight before substituting into p = F/A.

misconceptions.question: An area is given as 200 cm². What is it in m²?
misconceptions.correct: 0.02 m², because 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
misconceptions.misconception: The area can be put straight into p = F/A in whatever unit the question gives.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Length conversions are done automatically by now, so students forget that area needs the conversion squared.
misconceptions.correction: The area in p = F/A must be in metres squared. Divide an area in cm² by 10 000.

misconceptions.question: What unit is pressure measured in?
misconceptions.correct: The pascal, Pa.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure is measured in newtons, because pressure is just the push on something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure and force are used as synonyms in everyday language, and the newton is the force unit students know best.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals, Pa. Force alone is measured in newtons, N.

misconceptions.question: Which quantities appear in the equation for the pressure due to a column of liquid?
misconceptions.correct: Height of the column, density of the liquid and gravitational field strength.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure depends on the area of the column, because a wider column holds more liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: More liquid feels like more pressure, so students bring in the width or area of the container.
misconceptions.correction: p = h ρ g contains no area term. A wide tank and a narrow tube filled to the same height give the same pressure at the base.

misconceptions.question: Two tanks are filled to the same depth, one with water and one with mercury. Where is the pressure at the base greater?
misconceptions.correct: In the mercury, because mercury is much denser than water.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the depth matters; the liquid the column is made of makes no difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Depth is the variable students meet first and can feel in a swimming pool, so it crowds out density.
misconceptions.correction: Pressure is h × ρ × g. A denser liquid gives a heavier column above the point and so a greater pressure.

misconceptions.question: Why is the pressure greater deeper down in a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: There is a taller column of liquid above the point, so the weight above it is greater.
misconceptions.misconception: The liquid at the bottom is squashed into a smaller space, so it becomes denser and presses harder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the idea of compression from gases, where density really does change, to liquids.
misconceptions.correction: The density of a liquid is effectively constant. It is the greater height of liquid above the point that raises the pressure.

misconceptions.question: How do you rearrange p = h ρ g to find h?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the pressure by ρ g.
misconceptions.misconception: When applying or rearranging p = h ρ g, students perform the wrong operation with the ρ g factor: multiplying by ρ g when they should divide, dividing ρ g by the pressure, subtracting ρ g, dividing by g instead of multiplying, or dropping g altogether.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is done by pattern-matching rather than by inverting the operation.
misconceptions.correction: ρ and g multiply h, so to undo them you divide the pressure by ρ g.

misconceptions.question: What value of g should be used in a pressure calculation?
misconceptions.correct: The value printed in the question, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg.
misconceptions.misconception: g is always 10 N/kg, because that is the number we always use.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rounded values are used in early lessons and become fixed in memory.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the value of g will be given in any calculation, so read it from the question.

misconceptions.question: What unit must the density be in for p = h ρ g?
misconceptions.correct: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.
misconceptions.misconception: Density can be used in whatever unit it is given in, such as g/cm³.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Density is often measured in g/cm³ in practical work, so that unit feels equally valid.
misconceptions.correction: The equation as given in the specification requires density in kg/m³.

misconceptions.question: A diver goes from 8 m to 12 m deep. How is the increase in pressure found?
misconceptions.correct: Use the difference in depth, 4 m, in Δp = Δh ρ g.
misconceptions.misconception: Use the final depth in the equation, because that is where the diver ends up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The question mentions two depths, and students grab the one that seems to be 'the answer depth'.
misconceptions.correction: A difference in pressure comes from a difference in height, so substitute the change in depth.

misconceptions.question: Why does a submerged object experience an upthrust?
misconceptions.correct: The pressure on its bottom surface is greater than the pressure on its top surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The liquid underneath pushes up and nothing at all pushes down on the top.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only the upward result is remembered, so students drop the downward push that is being outweighed.
misconceptions.correction: There is a force on both surfaces. The bottom is deeper, so the pressure there is greater and the resultant force is upwards.

misconceptions.question: Why does a large steel ship float?
misconceptions.correct: Its overall density, including the air inside its hull, is less than the density of water.
misconceptions.misconception: Heavy things sink and light things float, so a heavy ship should sink.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday examples compare a stone with a cork without controlling for volume.
misconceptions.correction: Floating depends on density, not weight alone. A heavy object with a large volume can have a low density and float.

misconceptions.question: What is true of the forces on a floating object?
misconceptions.correct: The upthrust is equal to the weight of the object.
misconceptions.misconception: The upthrust must be bigger than the weight, or the object would not stay up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Floating up' is read as an unbalanced upward force rather than as equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: A floating object is in equilibrium, so the upthrust equals the weight. A larger upthrust would accelerate it upwards.

misconceptions.question: What is 4500 ÷ 0.03?
misconceptions.correct: 150000, because dividing by 0.03 is the same as multiplying by 100/3.
misconceptions.misconception: Dividing by 0.03 gives the same answer as dividing by 0.3, or by 3.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dividing by a number smaller than one is rare in everyday arithmetic, so the decimal point is dropped or shifted by the wrong number of places.
misconceptions.correction: Check the size of the answer: dividing by a number less than 1 must make the answer larger than the number you started with.

misconceptions.question: How big is the atmosphere compared with the Earth?
misconceptions.correct: It is a thin layer of air relative to the size of the Earth.
misconceptions.misconception: The atmosphere is a huge, deep blanket, far thicker than the Earth is wide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams exaggerate the atmosphere so it can be seen, and space feels limitless.
misconceptions.correction: The atmosphere is thin compared with the size of the Earth, and it fades out with altitude.

misconceptions.question: How does the density of the air change with altitude?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases; the atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude.
misconceptions.misconception: Air is air, so it has the same density everywhere in the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Air is invisible and feels identical everywhere a student has ever been.
misconceptions.correction: The atmosphere gets less dense with increasing altitude, which is why there is less air above a high surface.

misconceptions.question: Why is atmospheric pressure lower on a mountain top?
misconceptions.correct: There is less air above the surface, so fewer molecules collide with it.
misconceptions.misconception: Gravity is much weaker up a mountain, so the air presses down far less.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Height is associated with escaping gravity, as in pictures of astronauts floating.
misconceptions.correction: Gravity is almost unchanged over a few kilometres. What changes is the amount of air above the surface.

misconceptions.question: What causes atmospheric pressure at a surface?
misconceptions.correct: Air molecules colliding with the surface.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the wind: moving air blowing against a surface is what presses on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Wind is the only time students feel air pushing on them.
misconceptions.correction: Still air exerts pressure too, because its molecules are always colliding with the surface.

misconceptions.question: Why is the pressure lower at the top of a mountain?
misconceptions.correct: Less air lies above, so the weight of air above the surface is smaller.
misconceptions.misconception: The air up there is colder, and cold air presses less hard on a surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cold is the most obvious difference at altitude, so it is offered as the cause of everything.
misconceptions.correction: The change in pressure comes from the reduced amount of air above the surface, not from its temperature.

mcqs.stem: In physics, what is meant by the term 'fluid'?

options.text: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
options.rationale: The specification states that a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas; both can flow and both exert pressure.

options.text: A liquid only, since a gas cannot be poured.
options.rationale: Everyday use of 'fluid' means a runny liquid, so gases get ruled out.

options.text: Anything that pours, such as dry sand.
options.rationale: Pouring is taken as the test, which wrongly admits powders.

options.text: A gas only, as gases fill any space.
options.rationale: Students who tie 'fluid' to complete freedom of movement reserve the word for gases.

mcqs.stem: A sealed can holds compressed air. In which direction does the air pressure exert a force on the flat top of the can?

options.text: Vertically downwards, pulled by the air's weight.
options.rationale: Pressure is first met as an object resting on the ground, where the force is vertical.

options.text: At right angles to the top, pushing outwards.
options.rationale: The pressure in a fluid causes a force normal to any surface it touches.

options.text: Sideways across the top, following the airflow.
options.rationale: The push is assumed to follow the direction the air is moving in.

options.text: Inwards to the centre of the sealed can.
options.rationale: The gas is imagined pulling its container inwards, as if under tension.

mcqs.stem: Water in a reservoir presses on a sloping side wall. How does the force from the water act on that wall?

options.text: Vertically downwards all the way down the wall.
options.rationale: The weight of the water is assumed to set the direction of the force.

options.text: Straight downwards, in line with the water's weight.
options.rationale: Wrong: the force is normal to the wall, not vertical; reflects the belief that fluid pressure acts straight down under the water's weight.

options.text: Normal to the wall at every point along it.
options.rationale: Pressure in a fluid causes a force at right angles to the surface, whatever its angle.

options.text: Along the wall, the way the water runs.
options.rationale: Flow direction is confused with the direction of the pressure force.

mcqs.stem: Which equation gives the pressure at the surface of a fluid?

options.text: pressure = (area of that surface)/(force normal to that surface)
options.rationale: The division is remembered but inverted, putting area on the top.

options.text: pressure = (force normal to a surface) × (area of the surface)
options.rationale: A larger area is assumed to give a larger pressure, so the two are multiplied.

options.text: pressure = (force parallel to a surface)/(area of that surface)
options.rationale: The force is taken to act along the surface rather than at right angles to it.

options.text: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface)
options.rationale: This is the equation exactly as the specification states it: p = F/A.

mcqs.stem: A force of 4500 N acts at right angles to a surface of area 0.03 m². Calculate the pressure on the surface.

options.rationale: The decimal point slips: 4500 is divided by 0.3 rather than by 0.03.

options.text: 135 Pa
options.rationale: Force and area are multiplied instead of divided: 4500 x 0.03.
The decimal point is dropped altogether and the area is read as 3 m².

mcqs.stem: A crate presses on the floor with a force of 2400 N normal to the floor and exerts a pressure of 800 Pa. Calculate the area of contact.

options.text: 3 m²
30 m²
options.rationale: A place-value slip in the division: 2400 is divided by 80.
The rearrangement is inverted, giving 800/2400.
Force and pressure are multiplied, 2400 x 800.

mcqs.stem: In the equation p = F/A, what unit is the pressure p measured in?

options.text: Newton per metre, N/m.
options.rationale: Force per length is offered instead of force per unit area.

options.text: Newtons, written N.
options.rationale: Pressure is treated as another word for the pushing force.

options.text: Square metres, m².
options.rationale: The unit of the area in the equation is given as the unit of the answer.

options.text: Pascals, written Pa.
options.rationale: The specification gives pressure, p, in pascals, Pa.

mcqs.stem: A force of 16 N acts normal to a surface of area 200 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals. 1 m² = 10 000 cm²

options.text: 8 Pa
options.rationale: The area is converted by dividing by 100, giving 2 m².

options.text: 80 Pa
options.rationale: The area is converted by dividing by 1000, giving 0.2 m².

options.text: 800 Pa

options.rationale: The area in cm² is substituted with no conversion at all.

mcqs.stem: A brick of mass 2.0 kg rests flat on a bench. gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Which value is the force normal to the bench in p = F/A?

options.text: 19.6 N, the weight of the brick.
options.rationale: F must be a force in newtons: weight = 2.0 x 9.8 = 19.6 N.

options.text: 2.0 N, the mass rewritten in newtons.
options.rationale: The mass number is kept and the unit simply changed to newtons.

options.text: 9.8 N, the field strength in N/kg.
options.rationale: The only value already carrying newtons is taken as the force.

options.text: 0.20 N, the mass divided by g.
options.rationale: Mass and g are divided rather than multiplied.

mcqs.stem: A walker on soft snow puts on wide snowshoes and stops sinking in. Why?

options.text: The larger area increases the pressure on the snow.
options.rationale: Area is treated as increasing pressure rather than dividing the force.

options.text: The larger area reduces the pressure on the snow.
options.rationale: The normal force is unchanged but is spread over more area, so p = F/A falls.

options.text: The larger area presses down harder on the snow.
options.rationale: Wrong: larger area lowers pressure, not raises it; reflects the belief that more area means more pressure.

options.text: The force is the walker's mass, and wide shoes shrink it.
options.rationale: Wrong: area does not change the force; reflects conflating mass with the pressing force and imagining wide shoes reduce it.

mcqs.stem: Which word equation gives the pressure due to a column of liquid?

options.text: pressure = width of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
options.rationale: The width of the container is used in place of the height of the column.

options.text: pressure = height of the column × area of the column × gravitational field strength
options.rationale: Area is brought in because a wider column is assumed to press harder.

options.text: pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
options.rationale: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it.

options.text: pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid / gravitational field
options.rationale: The final multiplication is remembered as a division.

mcqs.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, how is the height h of the liquid column found from the other quantities?

options.text: Multiply the pressure by ρ g.
options.rationale: The equation is a product, so multiplication is repeated instead of undone.

options.text: Divide ρ g by the pressure value.
options.rationale: The division is carried out the wrong way round.

options.text: Subtract ρ g from the pressure.
options.rationale: The operation joining the quantities is misread as an addition.

options.text: Divide the pressure by ρ g.
options.rationale: ρ and g multiply h in p = h ρ g, so h = p divided by ρ g.

mcqs.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, which units must be used for p and for h?

options.text: p in pascals, Pa and h in centimetres, cm
options.rationale: Laboratory centimetres are assumed to be acceptable for the height.

options.text: p in pascals, Pa and h in metres, m
options.rationale: The specification gives pressure in pascals, Pa and height of the column in metres, m.

options.text: p in newtons, N and h in centimetres, cm
options.rationale: Both the pressure unit and the height unit are taken from everyday use.

options.text: p in newtons, N and h in metres, m
options.rationale: Pressure is confused with force, so the newton is chosen.

mcqs.stem: In the equation p = h ρ g, what unit must the density ρ be given in?

options.text: Kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.
options.rationale: The specification gives density, ρ, in kilograms per metre cubed, kg/m³.

options.text: Kilograms per litre, kg/l.
options.rationale: Area units are used because m² is the familiar unit from p = F/A.

options.text: Grams per centimetre cubed, g/cm³.
options.rationale: The unit used in practical density work is assumed to be acceptable here.

options.text: Newtons per metre cubed, N/m³.
options.rationale: Mass is confused with weight, so newtons replace kilograms.

mcqs.stem: An exam question asks for the pressure at the bottom of a column of sea water. What does the specification say about the gravitational field strength g?

options.text: It must be recalled from memory as 9.8 N/kg.
options.rationale: Recall of g is assumed to be required, as it is for some other constants.

options.text: It is measured in newtons, N, and is recalled.
options.rationale: The unit of g is confused with the unit of force.

options.text: It is always taken as exactly 10 N/kg here.
options.rationale: The rounded classroom value is treated as the only value.

options.text: Its value will be given in the question, in N/kg.
options.rationale: The specification states that in any calculation the value of g will be given.

mcqs.stem: Explain why the pressure at a point in a liquid increases as that point gets deeper.

options.text: The liquid becomes denser lower down, where it is squashed.
options.rationale: Compression of gases is transferred to liquids, whose density is effectively fixed.

options.text: The liquid flows downwards, pressing harder low down.
options.rationale: Wrong: pressure rises because a taller column lies above; reflects the belief that the force follows the direction the fluid flows.

options.text: A taller column of liquid lies above it, weighing more.
options.rationale: Pressure is h ρ g: a greater height of liquid above the point means more weight above it.

options.text: The container holds a lot more liquid low down than high up.
options.rationale: The total amount of liquid is used in place of the height above the point.

mcqs.stem: Two tanks are filled to the same depth, one with water and one with mercury. Why is the pressure at the base greater in the mercury?

options.text: Mercury is denser, so the column above weighs more.
options.rationale: In p = h ρ g the height is the same, so the greater density gives the greater pressure.

options.text: The mercury must be filled to a greater depth.
options.rationale: Wrong: both are at the same depth; the greater pressure comes from mercury's higher density, not from extra depth.

options.text: Mercury is denser, so its column is taller than water.
options.rationale: Density is confused with height, although both tanks are filled to the same depth.

options.text: Mercury fills up more volume at the same depth here.
options.rationale: Volume is brought in although the two tanks are identical.

mcqs.stem: Calculate the pressure due to a column of water of height 25 m. density of water = 1000 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

options.rationale: The height and density are divided by g instead of multiplied by it.
The gravitational field strength is left out of the calculation.

options.text: 245 Pa
options.rationale: The density of the water is left out of the calculation.

mcqs.stem: A diver swims from a depth of 8.0 m to a depth of 12.0 m. density of sea water = 1030 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Calculate the increase in pressure on the diver.

options.rationale: The density is left out of the calculation.
The final depth of 12.0 m is used instead of the change in depth.

options.text: 420 Pa
options.rationale: The product is divided by g rather than multiplied by it.

mcqs.stem: A sealed can is held completely under water. Why does the water exert a resultant upward force on it?

options.text: Water pushes up on the bottom and not down on the top.
options.rationale: The downward push on the top surface is forgotten altogether.

options.text: The can is full of air, which is lighter than the water.
options.rationale: Lightness of the contents is offered in place of a pressure difference.

options.text: Only the bottom face has water pushing on it.
options.rationale: Wrong: water pushes on every face; the resultant is upward because bottom pressure exceeds top, not because only the base is pushed.

options.text: Pressure on its bottom face exceeds that on its top.
options.rationale: The bottom face is deeper, so the pressure there is greater and the resultant force is upwards.

mcqs.stem: A submerged object experiences a greater pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface. What is the resultant upward force called?

options.text: The force by which upthrust beats weight.
options.rationale: Wrong: the resultant upward force is the upthrust itself, not a surplus over the weight.

options.text: The upthrust on the object.
options.rationale: The specification names this resultant upward force the upthrust.

options.text: A normal contact force from the water below.
options.rationale: Wrong: it is the upthrust, arising from a pressure difference, not a normal contact force from the water.

options.text: The water's push under its base only.
options.rationale: Wrong: the upward force is the upthrust from greater pressure below, not a push acting only on the underside.

mcqs.stem: A solid block is lowered into a tank of water and floats. Which statement explains why it floats?

options.text: Its density is lower than the density of the water.
options.rationale: Floating and sinking are decided by comparing the density of the object with that of the liquid.

options.text: It is lighter than water, whatever its size or shape.
options.rationale: Weight alone is used as the test, with no account taken of volume.

options.text: The upthrust on it is larger than its own weight.
options.rationale: Wrong: a floating object has upthrust equal to its weight; believing upthrust must exceed weight is a common error.

options.text: It has a large volume and holds a lot of air.
options.rationale: Volume alone is used, without comparing mass with volume.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere?

options.text: A deep layer of gas that gets denser as altitude rises.
options.rationale: The change of density with altitude is remembered but reversed.

options.text: A thick layer of air of the same density at all heights.
options.rationale: Air is assumed to be identical everywhere because it is invisible.

options.text: A layer of air about as deep as the Earth is wide.
options.rationale: Exaggerated diagrams leave students with a very deep atmosphere.

options.text: A thin layer of air round the Earth that thins with altitude.
options.rationale: The specification describes a thin layer, relative to the size of the Earth, that gets less dense with altitude.

mcqs.stem: Explain why atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain is lower than at sea level.

options.text: Gravity is much weaker at the top of a high mountain.
options.rationale: Height is associated with escaping gravity.

options.text: The air up there is colder, so it presses down less hard.
options.rationale: Cold is the most obvious difference at altitude, so it is offered as the cause.

options.text: There is less air above, so fewer molecules collide.
options.rationale: Fewer air molecules above the surface means less weight of air and fewer collisions with it.

options.text: The wind is stronger high up, blowing the air away.
options.rationale: Wind is taken to be the origin of atmospheric pressure.
